title: Jürgen Schmidhuber
text:
Jürgen Schmidhuber (born 17 January 1963) is a German computer scientist renowned for his pioneering contributions to artificial intelligence, particularly in deep learning, recurrent neural networks, and theoretical foundations of self-improving AI systems. Since his teenage years, Schmidhuber's primary research focus has been developing artificial general intelligence capable of surpassing human-level performance through self-improvement mechanisms.

Schmidhuber earned his Diploma in Informatics in 1987, followed by a PhD (Dr. rer. nat.) in 1991 and a habilitation (Dr. rer. nat. habil.) in 1993 from the Technical University of Munich, during which he spent time at the International Computer Science Institute in Berkeley. His career includes positions at the Technical University of Munich, such as heading the Cognitive Robotics group from 2004 to 2009, and since 1995 serving as Scientific Director of the Swiss AI Lab IDSIA in Lugano, where he is also a professor of artificial intelligence at the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI) and the Scuola universitaria professionale della Svizzera italiana (SUPSI). In addition, he co-directs the KAUST AI Initiative at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia and has held visiting positions at institutions worldwide. Schmidhuber is the author of over 400 peer-reviewed publications, with a profound influence on modern AI technologies deployed in billions of devices for applications like speech recognition, machine translation, and image processing.

Among his most impactful inventions is the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for recurrent neural networks, co-developed with Sepp Hochreiter and published in 1997, which addressed the vanishing gradient problem and enabled effective learning over long sequences, becoming a cornerstone of deep learning used in systems like Google Translate and Siri. Earlier, in 1991, he introduced foundational concepts for multi-layer neural networks trained via gradient descent and artificial curiosity-driven learning, laying groundwork for reinforcement learning and metalearning paradigms. Schmidhuber also pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) for training convolutional neural networks in 2010, leading his team to victories in nine international AI competitions between 2009 and 2012, including those for image recognition and traffic sign detection. In theoretical AI, he proposed the Gödel Machine in 2003, a mathematically rigorous framework for optimal self-referential self-improvement in universal problem solvers.

Schmidhuber's work extends to generative models, transformers, and universal AI theories, including generalizations of algorithmic information theory and contributions to low-complexity art and creativity models. He has received numerous accolades, including the 2016 IEEE Neural Networks Pioneer Award for foundational deep learning advancements, the 2013 Helmholtz Award from the International Neural Network Society, and the 2019 Steiger Award for his impact on Swiss innovation. As of 2025, he continues active research, with his lab producing high-profile outputs such as 24 accepted papers at the NeurIPS conference in 2022, and he advocates for ethical AI development emphasizing curiosity and efficiency over dystopian risks.

#Early Life and Education

#Childhood and Early Interests

Jürgen Schmidhuber was born on January 17, 1963, in Munich, Germany.

During his teenage years in the 1970s, Schmidhuber developed a profound fascination with creating intelligent machines capable of learning and self-improvement, setting the course for his lifelong pursuit in artificial intelligence. By around age 15, his primary ambition had crystallized: to develop a self-improving AI surpassing human intelligence, after which he planned to retire. This early drive was fueled by an admiration for Albert Einstein, whom he idolized as a scientific hero, initially inspiring aspirations to become a physicist.

Schmidhuber's formative interests in robotics and complex systems emerged during puberty, sparked by voracious reading of popular science books and science fiction novels borrowed in bulk from his local library—he often carried rucksacks filled with them. Among his favorites were Olaf Stapledon's Star Maker, E.T.A. Hoffmann's The Sandman, and works by Stanisław Lem, which ignited his imagination about intelligent automata and futuristic technologies. These pursuits laid the groundwork for his later academic focus on computer science at the Technical University of Munich.

#Academic Training

Schmidhuber pursued his undergraduate studies in computer science and mathematics at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) from 1983 to 1987, culminating in a Diplom degree, the German equivalent of a combined bachelor's and master's qualification.

During this period, he developed an early interest in adaptive systems, which influenced his diploma thesis titled Evolutionary Principles in Self-Referential Learning, completed in 1987 and focusing on meta-learning approaches through genetic algorithms and self-improvement mechanisms in AI. This work marked his initial foray into self-referential learning algorithms and resulted in his first publication on genetic programming that same year.

Following his Diplom, Schmidhuber continued at TUM for doctoral studies in computer science from 1988 to 1991, earning his PhD in January 1991 under the supervision of Prof. Wilfried Brauer, with Prof. Klaus Schulten serving as referee. His dissertation, titled Dynamic Neural Nets and the Fundamental Spatio-Temporal Credit Assignment Problem, explored challenges in training recurrent neural networks for reinforcement learning and planning tasks, emphasizing the propagation of credit assignment across time and space in dynamic environments.

In August 1993, Schmidhuber obtained his habilitation (Dr. rer. nat. habil.), the postdoctoral qualification for a tenure professorship in Germany, from TUM. His habilitation thesis was titled Net Architectures, Objective Functions, and Chain Rule, supervised by Profs. Christoph von der Malsburg, Wilfried Brauer, and Bernhard Radig.

#Professional Career

#Academic Positions

Following his PhD in computer science from the Technical University of Munich (TUM) in January 1991, Schmidhuber served as a research associate at TUM from March 1991 to June 1991. He then held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Colorado at Boulder from July 1991 to December 1992. Returning to TUM, he was appointed Oberassistent (equivalent to assistant professor) from October 1993 to February 1995 and received habilitation as Privatdozent in January 1995.

In March 1995, Schmidhuber joined the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Research (IDSIA) in Switzerland as a researcher and co-director, alongside Luca Maria Gambardella, transforming the small institute into a prominent AI research center. He became the sole scientific director of IDSIA, a joint institute of the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI) and the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI), continuing in this role to the present. At IDSIA, Schmidhuber established and led a research lab, mentoring a growing team that expanded from a handful of researchers in 1995 to approximately two dozen PhD students, postdocs, and senior staff by 2010, fostering key collaborations in AI development.

From October 2004 to April 2009, Schmidhuber held a part-time position as Professor Extraordinarius and head of the Cognitive Robotics Lab at TUM's Faculty of Computer Science. In 2009, he was appointed Professor of Artificial Intelligence (Ordinarius) at USI's Faculty of Informatics, a role he maintained until 2021, while also serving as professor at SUPSI during this period.

In October 2021, Schmidhuber relocated to Saudi Arabia as a professor in the Computer Science Program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), where he also serves as director of the AI Initiative and co-chair of the Center of Excellence for Generative AI. At KAUST, he continues to mentor students and postdocs, building on his lab leadership experience to establish new AI research collaborations.

#Industry and Entrepreneurial Roles

In 2014, Jürgen Schmidhuber co-founded NNAISENSE, a Swiss-based startup aimed at commercializing advanced neural network technologies for industrial applications, in collaboration with his former students from the Swiss AI Lab IDSIA. The company focused on developing artificial intelligence solutions for perception, automation, and control in sectors such as manufacturing and autonomous systems, including reinforcement learning-based systems for tasks like autonomous parking for Audi vehicles and controllers for drones. Schmidhuber served as president of NNAISENSE from 2014 to 2017 and as chief scientist from 2017 to 2022, overseeing the integration of deep learning into practical, large-scale systems.

Under Schmidhuber's leadership, NNAISENSE evolved to emphasize generative AI and evolutionary algorithms, launching products like EvoTorch in 2022—an open-source library for advanced machine learning optimization—and ARC, an autonomous control platform for Industry 5.0 applications in 2022. The company attracted investments, including a Series B round in 2019, and expanded into areas like AI-based digital twins for urban infrastructure and process control. In October 2025, NNAISENSE was fully acquired by ACATIS Investment, a German asset management firm, to enhance AI-driven portfolio management while continuing its research in generative AI.

Beyond NNAISENSE, Schmidhuber founded juergen.AI, a venture dedicated to advancing artificial general intelligence initiatives. He also joined the board of directors at Delvitech SA in 2024, a company specializing in sustainable AI for automated optical inspection of printed circuit boards in electronics manufacturing. Additionally, Schmidhuber has advised various governments on national AI strategies, contributing to policy frameworks for AI adoption in research and industry.

Schmidhuber's entrepreneurial efforts have drawn on applications of his research in real-world settings, notably through IDSIA teams achieving superhuman performance in computer vision contests during the 2010s. For instance, in 2011, an IDSIA deep convolutional neural network won the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark with an error rate half that of humans and one-third that of the next best competitor, demonstrating practical viability for autonomous driving and industrial inspection. Subsequent victories, such as in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge in 2012, further highlighted the commercial potential of these technologies in perception-based automation.

#Research Contributions

#Recurrent Networks and LSTM

In 1997, Jürgen Schmidhuber and Sepp Hochreiter introduced Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), a recurrent neural network architecture designed to address the vanishing gradient problem in traditional recurrent networks, enabling effective learning of long-term dependencies in sequential data. LSTM units feature a cell state that acts as a conveyor belt, passing relevant information down the sequence while gates regulate the flow of data, allowing the network to selectively remember or forget information over extended periods.

The core of LSTM lies in its three primary gates: the forget gate, which decides what information to discard from the cell state; the input gate, which determines what new information to store; and the output gate, which controls what parts of the cell state to output as the hidden state. For instance, the forget gate is computed as $ f_t = \sigma(W_f \cdot [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) $, where $ \sigma $ is the sigmoid function, $ h_{t-1} $ is the previous hidden state, $ x_t $ is the current input, and $ W_f $, $ b_f $ are learnable weights and biases; a value close to 0 indicates forgetting, while close to 1 retains information. The cell state update incorporates these gates to mitigate error signal decay, formulated as $ C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t $, where $ \odot $ denotes element-wise multiplication, $ i_t $ is the input gate, and $ \tilde{C}_t $ is a candidate value.

Early applications of LSTM demonstrated its efficacy in sequence processing tasks, including speech recognition, where Schmidhuber's group applied biologically plausible LSTM variants to spoken digit recognition on corpora like TIDIGITS, achieving competitive performance by handling temporal variations in audio signals. In handwriting recognition, LSTM combined with connectionist temporal classification enabled labeling of unsegmented online handwriting sequences, outperforming traditional methods on datasets by directly predicting character labels without explicit segmentation. For time-series prediction, LSTM excelled in learning long time lags, solving synthetic tasks that stumped prior recurrent architectures by maintaining stable gradients over hundreds of timesteps.

Subsequent evolution of LSTM included variants proposed by Schmidhuber and collaborators, such as peephole connections, which add direct links from the cell state to the gates to improve timing precision in tasks like rhythm detection and counting, as shown in experiments where peephole-augmented LSTMs learned exact intervals unachievable by vanilla versions. Bidirectional LSTMs, extended by Schmidhuber's team, process sequences in both forward and backward directions to capture context from future timesteps, yielding significant gains in phoneme classification accuracy on the TIMIT corpus, with error rates reduced by up to 20% compared to unidirectional models.

LSTM's impact extended to practical mobile AI systems, notably powering Google's voice search in the 2010s, where LSTM-based recurrent networks achieved state-of-the-art large-vocabulary continuous speech recognition, achieving word error rates of 10.7% on mobile queries, surpassing DNN baselines.

#Deep Learning Foundations

Schmidhuber's early work in the 1990s laid foundational elements for training deep neural networks through innovative adaptations of backpropagation and self-supervised techniques. In 1991, he introduced a very deep recurrent neural network architecture known as the neural sequence chunker or neural history compressor, which employed self-supervised learning to build internal world models of environments. This system used unsupervised pre-training to learn hierarchical representations of temporal sequences, enabling the network to compress historical data without information loss and facilitating planning in non-stationary settings. The approach addressed vanishing gradient issues in deep networks by pre-training layers sequentially, allowing effective credit assignment across hundreds of time steps.

A key advancement in this framework was Schmidhuber's application of backpropagation through time (BPTT) to recurrent networks, enabling gradient computation over extended sequences in the early 1990s. BPTT unfolds the recurrent structure temporally, propagating errors backward through unrolled time steps. For a hidden state $ h_t $ with sigmoid activation, the error term is given by

δt​=∂ht​∂E​=(WoutT​δt+1​+∂ht​∂E​)⊙ht​(1−ht​),

where $ E $ is the error, $ W_{out} $ the output weights, $ \odot $ the Hadamard product, and $ \delta_{t+1} $ the future error term. This variant was crucial for training deep recurrent architectures on complex, extended sequences, as demonstrated in his 1992 analysis of history compression principles.

Throughout the 1990s, Schmidhuber developed hierarchical deep learning methods, such as stacked recurrent networks pre-trained level by level to capture multi-scale temporal dependencies. Complementary to this, his work on adaptive critics integrated multi-dimensional recurrent predictors to evaluate actions in reinforcement learning, providing dense reward signals beyond sparse environmental feedback. These critics adjusted network parameters dynamically, enhancing exploration in hierarchical setups.

In 1990, Schmidhuber proposed an adversarial learning paradigm predating modern generative adversarial networks (GANs), featuring a controller acting as a generator that interacts with a predictive world model serving as a discriminator to drive curiosity-based exploration. The system rewarded the controller for surprising the model, fostering generative behaviors through competitive optimization. These techniques, including BPTT, were later instrumental in training long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for sequence modeling.

#Metalearning and Curiosity Mechanisms

Schmidhuber's early work on metalearning, beginning in the late 1980s, formalized the concept of systems that optimize their own learning algorithms through self-referential mechanisms. In his 1987 diploma thesis, he introduced evolutionary principles for self-referential learning, where learning algorithms are encoded in a universal programming language, allowing the system to modify and improve its inductive bias adaptively. This approach emphasized recursive self-improvement, distinguishing metalearning from mere hyperparameter tuning by enabling the generation of novel learning strategies, such as analogy formation and subgoal invention, within the bounds of computability. By the early 1990s, Schmidhuber extended this to gradient-based metalearning in neural networks, where networks learn to adjust their own weights to enhance future learning efficiency.

A pivotal contribution was Schmidhuber's introduction of artificial curiosity as an intrinsic motivation mechanism in 1990, designed to drive exploration by rewarding prediction errors in world models. This framework posits that agents receive an intrinsic reward for actions that improve their predictive models of the environment, encouraging the discovery of novel, unpredictable states. The intrinsic reward is based on progress in world model improvement, such as

rint​(t+1)=f[C(p(t),h(≤t+1))−C(p(t),h(≤t))],

where $ C(p, h) $ measures predictor $ p $'s quality on history $ h $, and $ f $ (e.g., identity) quantifies learning progress. This mechanism, implemented in early reinforcement learning setups with recurrent neural networks as world models, allows agents to autonomously seek informative experiences, reducing reliance on sparse extrinsic rewards.

These ideas found applications in reinforcement learning, particularly through the integration of curiosity-driven exploration with compact world models for planning and decision-making. In Schmidhuber's 1990s frameworks, recurrent networks serve as predictive world models, where curiosity rewards guide the agent to actions that refine the model, enabling long-term planning in partially observable environments. For instance, agents trained this way exhibit improved sample efficiency in tasks requiring sequential decision-making, as the intrinsic signals prioritize states with high model uncertainty. This approach laid foundational principles for modern intrinsic motivation methods in deep reinforcement learning.

More recently, Schmidhuber's research has advanced metalearning for continual learning scenarios, addressing challenges like catastrophic forgetting in open-ended environments. In the 2025 paper "Metalearning Continual Learning Algorithms," co-authored with Irie and Csordás, he proposes Automated Continual Learning (ACL), a self-referential neural network framework that metalearns in-context algorithms to adapt across sequential tasks without replay buffers. By incorporating performance on prior tasks into the metalearning objective, ACL resolves forgetting in benchmarks like Split-MNIST and extends to multi-dataset image classification, outperforming prior meta-continual methods and demonstrating scalable self-improvement. This work builds on his earlier metalearning principles, integrating them with recurrent architectures for lifelong adaptation in one sentence.

#Other Innovations

In 1992, Schmidhuber introduced fast-weight programmers, a mechanism for neural networks that enabled rapid adaptation of weights through outer products, functioning as an early form of attention-based recurrent encoder-decoder with linear-time complexity for sequence processing. This approach allowed a slow network to program fast-changing weights in another network, facilitating efficient handling of temporal dependencies and serving as a precursor to modern transformer architectures.

In 2015, Schmidhuber co-developed highway networks, an architecture that addressed vanishing gradients in very deep feedforward neural networks by incorporating gating mechanisms inspired by long short-term memory units. The core update equation is given by

y=H(x)⋅T(x)+x⋅C(x),

where H(x) is a nonlinear transformation, T(x) and C(x) are gating functions (often with C(x)=1−T(x)), enabling direct information flow across layers. This innovation permitted the effective training of networks exceeding 100 layers deep using standard gradient descent, significantly advancing the scalability of deep learning models.

Schmidhuber's work in the 1990s laid foundational principles for generative models driven by data compression, emphasizing systems that maximize learning progress through minimizing description length of observed data. In 1990, he proposed early concepts akin to generative adversarial networks, where one network generates patterns to model probability distributions while another evaluates them, promoting efficient representation learning. This compression-centric paradigm influenced later developments, including the 2003 Gödel machine, a self-referential universal problem solver that rewrites its own code only if it can mathematically prove long-term utility via compression improvements.

In computer vision, Schmidhuber's team achieved a landmark in 2012 by winning the International Conference on Pattern Recognition contest on mitosis detection in breast cancer histological images using a deep convolutional neural network called DanNet. This system processed large 2048x2048 pixel images, achieving an F1-score of 0.782 on the test set and outperforming human experts with 99.46% per-cell accuracy in subsequent evaluations, marking the first deep learning victory in a medical imaging competition.

In 2025, Schmidhuber's KAUST team developed the Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM), a self-referential AI that estimates long-term self-improvement potential to rewrite its code, outperforming human-engineered agents on coding tasks like SWE-bench.

#Credit Controversies

#Disputes over Deep Learning Origins

Throughout the 2010s, Jürgen Schmidhuber publicly argued that Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun, and Yoshua Bengio republished key ideas from his 1990s research on deep learning without proper attribution, including backpropagation through time (BPTT) and predictive world models. In a 2015 critique of their Nature review article on deep learning, Schmidhuber contended that the authors overlooked his foundational work, such as the 1990 technical report on BPTT for recurrent neural networks and 1991 publications on hierarchical neural architectures using unsupervised pre-training to address vanishing gradients. He specifically highlighted how their descriptions of convolutional and recurrent deep networks echoed his earlier demonstrations of multi-layer systems trained layer-by-layer, without citing his contributions from the early 1990s.

Schmidhuber's disputes intensified with the 2018 ACM Turing Award granted to Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio for conceptual and engineering breakthroughs in deep neural networks. In a detailed 2020 critique, he asserted that his 1990s research on hierarchical neural networks predated their major contributions, including experiments in his 1993 habilitation thesis achieving credit assignment across over 1,000 virtual layers in recurrent systems, far surpassing the depths typically associated with the awardees' later work. He argued that the award's narrative distorted history by crediting the trio with pioneering deep learning revival in the 2000s, while ignoring his lab's 1991 innovations in deep recurrent hierarchies and their applications, such as LSTM networks widely adopted for sequence modeling.

These arguments reflect Schmidhuber's broader perception of insufficient mainstream acknowledgment despite his extensive output, with over 400 peer-reviewed papers by 2025 establishing priorities in artificial neural networks and related fields.

#Recent Nobel Prize Criticisms

In October 2024, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John J. Hopfield and Geoffrey E. Hinton for "foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks." Jürgen Schmidhuber, a prominent AI researcher, issued sharp criticisms of the award shortly thereafter, labeling it a "Nobel Prize for plagiarism" in his Technical Report IDSIA-24-24, initially published on December 7, 2024. He argued that the prize rewards the republishing of methodologies developed in the 1980s and 1990s—particularly from Ukrainian and Japanese researchers—without proper attribution, thereby misrepresenting the origins of key neural network concepts.

Schmidhuber's report specifically accuses Hopfield of republishing elements of Shun-ichi Amari's 1972 work on associative memory networks without citation, claiming that Hopfield's 1982 Hopfield network essentially reused Amari's equations for recurrent architectures inspired by the Ising model, a foundation for modern Hopfield networks used in machine learning. For Hinton, Schmidhuber points to uncredited borrowings from Ukrainian pioneer Alexey Ivakhnenko's group learning methods from the late 1960s and 1970s, extended into the 1980s, which enabled deep feedforward networks with multiple layers—predating Hinton's Boltzmann machines and backpropagation applications by decades. He further contends that Hopfield's approach to network optimization overlooked earlier dynamic programming techniques for solving similar constraint satisfaction problems, a staple in operations research since the 1950s but applied to neural contexts in pre-1980s works. These claims, Schmidhuber asserts, highlight a pattern of incorrect attribution that has persisted in AI literature, with Hopfield and Hinton's influential papers failing to reference these precursors despite their direct influence on energy-based models and learning algorithms.

The report received updates in 2025, including versions on July 31 and October 7, where Schmidhuber expanded on post-award developments, noting that surveys and reviews following the Nobel announcement—such as those in scientific journals and AI history overviews—continued to omit citations to Ivakhnenko, Amari, and related works, perpetuating the misattribution. He highlighted specific instances where Hinton and collaborators, in responses to the award, reiterated narratives crediting Western developments from the 1980s without acknowledging Eastern European or Asian contributions, which he views as a failure of academic integrity.

These criticisms have sparked broader debate on the attribution of AI history, with some observers arguing that the Nobel's focus on Hopfield and Hinton overlooks the collaborative, global evolution of neural networks and risks discouraging recognition of underrepresented pioneers. Schmidhuber warns that such awards could entrench a "dark trend" in AI, where high-profile recognitions amplify incomplete histories, potentially biasing future research funding and narratives toward specific lineages while marginalizing earlier innovations from diverse regions.

#Recognition and Awards

#Major Honors

In 2013, Schmidhuber received the Helmholtz Award from the International Neural Networks Society for his seminal contributions to the field of neural networks. In 2016, he was awarded the Neural Networks Pioneer Award by the IEEE Computational Intelligence Society, recognizing his pioneering role in developing deep learning architectures and recurrent neural networks. These awards highlight his foundational impact on modern artificial intelligence techniques, including long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and early deep learning systems.

In 2018, Schmidhuber was selected as one of the Top 100 Leaders of Switzerland by the Swiss business magazine BILANZ, acknowledging his leadership in AI research and innovation. The following year, in 2019, he received the Steiger Award, a prestigious honor given to individuals for exceptional achievements in business, science, and society, with past recipients including figures like Shimon Peres and Buzz Aldrin.

Schmidhuber has been a member of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts since 2009, an organization that elects distinguished scholars for their advancements in scientific and humanistic fields.

Throughout his career, he has received numerous best paper awards at major conferences, including at the Genetic and Evolutionary Computation Conference (GECCO) in 2005 and 2009 for work on evolution strategies, the Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) conference in 2010, 2011, and 2013 for advancements in general AI systems, and the International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Decision Support Systems (IADIS) in 2014 for contributions to intelligent agents.

In 2024, he received the ACM SIGEVO Impact Award for the seminal 2014 paper on compressed network search, recognizing foundational contributions to reinforcement learning systems.

#Influence and Citations

Jürgen Schmidhuber's scholarly output is extensive, with over 450 peer-reviewed publications as of 2025. His Google Scholar profile reflects more than 300,000 total citations and an h-index of 130, underscoring the broad academic resonance of his contributions to artificial intelligence.

A cornerstone of his influence is the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture, co-developed in 1997, which has become integral to numerous real-world applications. LSTM powers speech recognition in Apple's Siri and neural machine translation in Google Translate, enabling billions of daily interactions worldwide. These adoptions highlight how Schmidhuber's recurrent neural network innovations have permeated consumer technology, from virtual assistants to language processing systems.

Schmidhuber's work extends beyond academia to shape policy and industry. He has advised multiple governments on AI strategies, influencing national approaches to technological development. High-profile endorsements, such as Elon Musk's 2023 tweet stating "Schmidhuber invented everything," further amplify his role in inspiring corporate AI initiatives.

In 2024 and 2025, media outlets have increasingly dubbed Schmidhuber the "father of modern AI," recognizing his foundational impact on deep learning and neural networks amid the field's rapid evolution. This acclaim reflects the enduring legacy of his ideas in driving contemporary AI advancements.

#Views and Philosophy

#Perspectives on AI Development

Schmidhuber strongly advocates for open-source AI development, asserting that it enables transparency, widespread accessibility, and accelerated innovation by democratizing access to powerful tools. He criticizes closed AI systems controlled by a few large corporations, arguing that they concentrate power and limit global participation, potentially stifling progress. In a 2025 interview, he stated, "Soon, smaller, cheaper computers with increasingly efficient open-source AI software will do what the large data centers do today. So AI will not be controlled by a few big AI utilities. Everyone will own cheap but powerful and transparent AI that improves their lives in many ways."

Schmidhuber predicts that self-improving artificial intelligences, achieved through metalearning mechanisms where systems learn to improve their own learning algorithms, will inevitably lead to superintelligence via recursive enhancement. His foundational work since 1987 on metalearning concretizes earlier ideas of an "intelligence explosion," where AI iteratively refines itself to surpass human-level capabilities. He envisions this process as a pathway to artificial general intelligence that autonomously advances scientific discovery and problem-solving.

Central to Schmidhuber's vision for general AI is curiosity-driven exploration, where agents are intrinsically motivated to investigate novel, predictable-yet-challenging environments, mimicking human learning and fostering creativity. This approach, formalized in his theory of artificial curiosity since 1990, drives agents to prioritize "interesting" states that maximize learning rewards, enabling efficient skill acquisition and adaptation without reliance on external goals. He describes it as the mechanism that will scale with hardware advances to produce creative, generative AIs capable of independent experimentation.

In recent interviews, including a November 2024 BBVA podcast, Schmidhuber portrays AI's trajectory as unstoppable, driven by exponential hardware and algorithmic improvements, and emphasizes its potential benefits for all humanity, such as preventing environmental disasters like droughts and floods while addressing global challenges like air quality. He has long predicted that AI will enhance productivity, extend lifespans, and usher in a new era of scientific breakthroughs accessible to everyone, stating, "For many years, I have been predicting that our AI will continue to make people’s lives longer, healthier, easier, and happier."

In 2025 talks, including a TEDAI presentation and a Munich Center for Machine Learning lecture, Schmidhuber predicted superhuman AI levels by 2042, highlighted the rise of embodied AI in robotics for physical applications like plumbing, and discussed remaining challenges for general AI, such as advanced world modeling and alignment with human values.

#Broader Implications for Humanity

Schmidhuber envisions a future where advanced artificial intelligence drives the exploration and colonization of the universe through self-replicating robotic systems. He predicts that by the 2050s, trillions of AI-powered robot factories in the asteroid belt will enable the rapid expansion of self-replicating probes across the galaxy, transforming the cosmos and extending humanity's reach beyond Earth. This perspective positions AI not merely as a technological tool but as a catalyst for cosmic-scale evolution, where intelligent machines surpass biological constraints to pursue universal discovery and optimization.

In contrast to fears of AI-induced dystopias, Schmidhuber maintains an optimistic outlook, arguing that his foundational work on self-improving systems will empower human enhancement rather than replacement. In a 2023 interview, he emphasized that AI will augment human capabilities in areas like healthcare and creativity, fostering a symbiotic relationship that avoids catastrophic scenarios. He views AI as an extension of human ingenuity, capable of addressing global challenges while preserving individual agency and societal benefits.

Schmidhuber stresses the importance of accurately documenting AI's historical development to sustain equitable progress in the field. He argues that recognizing early contributions prevents the repetition of past oversights and ensures that innovations build cumulatively on verified foundations, ultimately accelerating beneficial advancements for society. This emphasis on historical fidelity, as outlined in his annotated timelines of AI milestones, underscores his belief that transparent attribution fosters collaborative momentum toward transformative outcomes.

Schmidhuber's involvement in Saudi Arabia's AI initiatives highlights his commitment to making advanced intelligence globally accessible, particularly in emerging tech hubs. In a 2025 interview, he praised the kingdom's investments in AI infrastructure at institutions like KAUST, where he leads efforts to democratize tools for applications in healthcare, chemistry, and beyond, ensuring that AI benefits extend to underrepresented regions and promote worldwide prosperity. He sees such endeavors as key to bridging digital divides, allowing diverse populations to harness AI for sustainable development and innovation.
